subject: Automotive & EVs
title: EV Affordability Gap
description: A short lesson to help you apply EV Affordability Gap.

hook.text: The average new EV still costs more upfront than the average gas car. That gap matters.

buildup.text: Battery costs make up 30–40% of an EV's price. Until those drop further, sticker prices stay high.

discovery.text: Lifetime costs often favor EVs—cheaper fuel, less maintenance, fewer moving parts to break.

twist.text: But many buyers can't afford the upfront premium, even if long-term costs are lower.

climax.text: Used EVs and sub-$25,000 models from China are starting to close the affordability gap globally.

punchline.text: EVs win on cost over time, but lose at the cash register.

quiz.question: What makes up 30-40% of an EV's price?

details.summary: Electric vehicles remain significantly more expensive than comparable gasoline cars, with the average new EV costing over $50,000, creating a barrier that prevents mass adoption among middle and lower-income buyers.
details.whyItMatters: EVs will only achieve mass adoption when they cost the same as or less than gasoline cars. The affordability gap delays the environmental benefits of electrification and creates an equity issue.
takeaways: The average new EV costs roughly $10,000 more than a comparable gas car
Battery costs must fall below $100 per kWh for price parity
Chinese manufacturers are closest to achieving affordable EVs

faq.question: When will electric cars be as cheap as gasoline cars?
faq.answer: Most analysts predict purchase price parity by 2027 to 2030 as battery costs continue declining. When total cost of ownership including fuel and maintenance is considered, some EVs are already cheaper over their lifetime.

faq.question: Are there any truly affordable EVs available today?
faq.answer: In China, BYD's Seagull sells for under $10,000. In the US and Europe, options are limited but growing. The Chevrolet Equinox EV and upcoming models target the $30,000 range before tax incentives.
